reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines
clinicalPearls: A benign, ACTH-independent cortical adenoma that autonomously secretes cortisol, producing the commonest surgically curable cause of endogenous, non-pituitary (adrenal) Cushing syndrome

The clinical spectrum ranges from florid Cushing syndrome (central obesity, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, wide violaceous striae, proximal myopathy, thin skin and easy bruising) to mild autonomous cortisol secretion detected incidentally on imaging

Because cortisol secretion is autonomous, plasma ACTH is suppressed and the contralateral adrenal and the unaffected ipsilateral cortex undergo atrophy, which is why postoperative glucocorticoid replacement is mandatory

The overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test is the pivotal screen: failure of morning cortisol to suppress, together with low or undetectable ACTH, points to an autonomously functioning adrenal source

Loss of circadian rhythm with a raised late-night salivary or midnight serum cortisol, and increased urinary free cortisol, corroborate hypercortisolism; a suppressed DHEA-sulphate is a useful pointer to a benign cortisol-producing adenoma

Cross-sectional imaging typically shows a well-defined, lipid-rich unilateral mass with low unenhanced attenuation and rapid contrast washout on CT, features that favour a benign adenoma over carcinoma or phaeochromocytoma

Even mild autonomous cortisol secretion is not harmless, being associated with hypertension, dysglycaemia, dyslipidaemia, osteoporosis and increased cardiovascular and mortality risk, so it warrants active assessment rather than simple reassurance
Laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy is the definitive treatment for a unilateral adenoma, with perioperative and postoperative steroid cover until the suppressed axis recovers
reference.pathophysiology: A cortisol-producing adenoma is a monoclonal benign neoplasm of the adrenal zona fasciculata that synthesises glucocorticoid independently of pituitary ACTH. Constitutive activation of the cyclic AMP / protein kinase A signalling pathway, frequently through somatic activating variants in PRKACA (and in some tumours changes in GNAS, CTNNB1 or components of the PKA pathway), drives steroidogenesis regardless of physiological feedback. The resulting chronic cortisol excess suppresses hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone and pituitary ACTH, so circulating ACTH falls and the non-tumorous adrenal tissue, including the contralateral gland, atrophies. Sustained glucocorticoid excess then produces the multisystem features of Cushing syndrome through catabolic effects on skin, muscle and bone, insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis, mineralocorticoid-like and vascular effects raising blood pressure, and immunosuppressive and neuropsychiatric consequences.
additionalDifferentials: Ectopic ACTH syndrome from a neuroendocrine tumour
ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia or primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease
Pseudo-Cushing states such as severe obesity, uncontrolled diabetes, depression or alcohol excess
additionalInvestigations: Overnight or formal low-dose dexamethasone suppression test with paired plasma ACTH
Late-night salivary cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol to confirm loss of circadian rhythm and hypercortisolism
Plasma ACTH and DHEA-sulphate to establish ACTH-independence and support a benign adenoma
Dedicated adrenal CT with unenhanced attenuation and contrast washout, or chemical-shift MRI, to characterise the mass
Biochemical exclusion of co-secreting phaeochromocytoma (plasma or urinary metanephrines) before any surgery
Assessment of complications: blood pressure, glucose and HbA1c, lipids and bone mineral density
In equivocal or bilateral disease, adrenal venous sampling or additional functional imaging to lateralise the source
redFlags: Rapid onset or rapidly progressive Cushingoid features, marked virilisation or a large or heterogeneous mass suggesting adrenocortical carcinoma
Severe hypokalaemic alkalosis with very high cortisol, raising concern for ectopic ACTH secretion
Hypertensive crisis, palpitations or headache suggesting an unrecognised co-existing phaeochromocytoma
Postoperative adrenal insufficiency (hypotension, hyponatraemia, collapse) if glucocorticoid cover is inadequate
New psychosis, severe infection or venous thromboembolism complicating florid hypercortisolism
reference.prognosis: Unilateral adrenalectomy is usually curative for a benign cortisol-producing adenoma, with resolution of hypercortisolism and gradual improvement in metabolic, skeletal and cardiovascular consequences, although recovery of the suppressed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis may take many months and requires interim steroid replacement. Untreated or long-standing cortisol excess, including mild autonomous secretion, carries excess cardiovascular, metabolic, skeletal and mortality risk.
pitfalls: Attributing an incidentally found adrenal mass to a non-functioning lesion without screening for autonomous cortisol secretion
Omitting or under-dosing postoperative glucocorticoid replacement, precipitating an adrenal crisis from the atrophic contralateral gland
Failing to exclude phaeochromocytoma with metanephrines before adrenalectomy
Misreading a pseudo-Cushing state as true endogenous hypercortisolism, or vice versa, without confirmatory dynamic testing
Overlooking features that suggest adrenocortical carcinoma rather than a benign adenoma and delaying appropriate oncological management
